butir.teks: An Explanation of the Praiseworthy Measure of the Praiseworthy Branches of Knowledge

Know that knowledge, in this respect, is of three kinds: a kind that is blameworthy, whether little or much of it; a kind that is praiseworthy, whether little or much of it, and the more of it there is, the better and more excellent; and a kind of which only the amount that suffices is praised, while going beyond it and exhaustive pursuit of it are not praised. It is like

the states of the body. Some of them are such that a little and a lot are both praised, like health and beauty; some are such that a little and a lot are both blamed, like ugliness and bad character; and some are such that moderation in them is praised, like spending money, for extravagance is not praised in it, even though it is a form of spending, and like courage, for recklessness is not praised in it, even though it is of the same kind as courage. Knowledge is likewise.

The kind that is blameworthy, whether little or much of it, is that which has no benefit in religion or in this world, since it contains harm that outweighs its benefit, like the knowledge of magic, talismans, and astrology. Some of it has no benefit at all, and spending life on it, which is the most precious thing a person owns, is a waste, and wasting what is precious is blameworthy.
And some of it contains harm that exceeds what is thought to be gained through it by way of fulfilling a need in this world, for that is not counted in comparison with the harm resulting from it.

As for the kind that is praiseworthy up to the furthest limits of exhaustive pursuit, it is knowledge of Allah Most High, His attributes, His acts, His way with His creation, and His wisdom in arranging the Hereafter upon this world. For this is knowledge sought for its own sake and as a means of reaching the happiness of the Hereafter. Exerting one's capacity in it to the utmost effort falls short of the required limit, for it is the sea whose depth cannot be reached; those who circle around it only hover around its shores and edges, to the extent made easy for them, and none has plunged into its edges except the prophets, the friends of Allah (awliya'), and those firmly grounded in knowledge, according to the differences in their ranks, in accordance with the differences in their strength and the varying of the decree of Allah Most High concerning them. This is the hidden knowledge that is not written down in books. What helps one to become alert to it is learning and witnessing the states of the scholars of the Hereafter, as their sign will be given later; this is at the beginning of the matter. And what helps toward it in the end is spiritual struggle (mujahada), spiritual discipline (riyada), purifying the heart and emptying it of worldly attachments, and emulating the prophets and the friends of Allah in this, so that it becomes clear through it to everyone who strives to seek it, in proportion to his provision and not in proportion to his effort; but there is no dispensing with striving in it. Spiritual struggle is the key of guidance; it has no key other than it. As for the branches of knowledge of which only a specific measure is praised, they are the branches of knowledge that we set out under the communal obligations (fard kifaya), for in each of them there is a bare minimum (iqtisar), which is the least; a moderate level (iqtisad), which is the middle; and exhaustive pursuit (istiqsa') beyond that moderate level, which has no limit up to the end of life. So be one of two men: either occupied with yourself, or free for others after being finished with yourself. And beware of busying yourself with what reforms others before reforming yourself. If you are the one occupied with yourself, then occupy yourself only with the knowledge that is obligatory upon you according to what your condition requires, and what of it relates to outward actions, such as learning the prayer, purification, and fasting. What is truly more important, which everyone has neglected, is the knowledge of the qualities of the heart, those that are praised and those that are blamed, since no human being is free of blameworthy qualities such as greed, envy, showing off (riya'), arrogance, self-admiration ('ujb), and their like. All of these are destructive, and neglecting them is among the obligatory duties, while occupying oneself with outward actions resembles occupying oneself with smearing the outside of the body when suffering from scabies and boils, and being lax about removing the morbid matter by bloodletting and purging. The superficial among the scholars advise outward actions, just as the run-of-the-mill physicians advise smearing the outside of the body, whereas the scholars of the Hereafter advise only purifying the inner and cutting off the sources of evil by destroying the places where it grows and uprooting its plantings from the heart. Most people resort to outward actions instead of purifying hearts because of the ease of the actions of the limbs and finding the actions of hearts difficult, just as one who finds drinking bitter medicines difficult resorts to smearing the outside. He keeps on wearying himself with smearing, while the morbid matter increases and the diseases are multiplied by it. So if you desire the Hereafter, seek salvation, and flee from eternal destruction, then occupy yourself with the knowledge of the inner ailments and their treatment, as we detailed in the Quarter on Destructive Traits. Then that will lead you, inevitably, to the praiseworthy stations (maqamat) mentioned in the Quarter on Saving Traits. For when the heart is emptied of what is blameworthy, it is filled with what is praiseworthy, and when the land is cleared of weeds, various kinds of crops and sweet herbs grow in it, but if it is not emptied of that, it does not grow those. So do not occupy yourself with the communal obligations, especially since among the mass of people there are those who have undertaken them. For one who destroys himself in what brings about the good of others is foolish. How great is the folly of one into whom vipers and scorpions have entered beneath his clothes and are set on killing him, while he looks for a fly-whisk with which to ward off flies from someone else who will neither avail him nor save him from what he meets from those snakes and scorpions when they set upon him.
And if you have finished with yourself and its purification, and are able to abandon sin, both outward and inward, and that has become a constant practice

for you and an easy habit in you (and how far that is from you!), then occupy yourself with the communal obligations and observe gradualness in them. Begin with the Book of Allah Most High, then the Sunna of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him), then the knowledge of Qur'anic exegesis (tafsir) and the rest of the sciences of the Qur'an, such as the knowledge of the abrogating and the abrogated, the separated and the connected, the clear and the ambiguous; and likewise for the Sunna. Then occupy yourself with the branches, which is the knowledge of the school (madhhab) from jurisprudence (fiqh), without disputation; then legal theory (usul al-fiqh), and so on to the remaining branches of knowledge, as far as life allows and time helps. Do not spend your whole life on a single discipline of them in seeking exhaustive pursuit, for knowledge is vast and life is short. These branches of knowledge are tools and preliminaries and are not sought for themselves but for something else; and whatever is sought for something else, the goal must not be forgotten in it, nor should one pile up much of it. So limit yourself, of the common knowledge of language, to what lets you understand the speech of the Arabs and speak it, and of its rare words to the rare words of the Qur'an and the rare words of hadith, and leave deep probing into it. And limit yourself, of grammar, to what relates to the Book and the Sunna. For there is no branch of knowledge but has a bare minimum, a moderate level, and exhaustive pursuit.

We point to these in hadith, Qur'anic exegesis, jurisprudence, and theology, so that you may measure others by them. The bare minimum in exegesis is what amounts to twice the Qur'an in size, as Ali al-Wahidi an-Naysaburi compiled it, namely al-Wajiz; and the moderate level is what amounts to three times the Qur'an, as compiled in al-Wasit on this subject; and what is beyond that is exhaustive pursuit that one can do without, with no limit up to the end of life.
As for hadith, the bare minimum in it is acquiring what is in the two Sahihs, by correcting a copy with a man who is expert in the knowledge of the text of hadith.

As for memorizing the names of the men, you have been spared that by what those before you have carried on your behalf, and you may rely on their books. Nor are you required to memorize the texts of the two Sahihs, but you should acquire them in such a way that you are able to look up what you need when the need arises. As for the moderate level in it, it is to add to the two of them what was transmitted outside them, of what is found in the authentic musnads.

As for exhaustive pursuit, it is what is beyond that, up to comprehending everything that has been transmitted, weak and strong, sound and unsound, together with knowing the many routes of transmission and knowing the circumstances of the men, their names, and their descriptions.

As for jurisprudence, the bare minimum in it is what the Mukhtasar of al-Muzani, may Allah have mercy on him, contains, which is what we arranged in Khulasat al-Mukhtasar; the moderate level in it is what reaches three times its like, which is the amount we set out in al-Wasit on the school; and exhaustive pursuit is what we set out in al-Basit, up to what lies beyond that of the lengthy works.

As for theology, its aim is only to defend the beliefs that the People of the Sunna transmitted from the righteous early generations, and nothing else; what lies beyond that is seeking to uncover the realities of things by other than their proper way. And for the aim of preserving the Sunna, the rank of the bare minimum of it is attained by a concise creed, which is the amount we set out in the Book of the Foundations of the Creeds, as part of this book. The moderate level in it is what reaches the amount of about a hundred leaves, which is what we set out in the book al-Iqtisad fi al-I'tiqad; it is needed for debating an innovator and countering his innovation with what invalidates it and removes it from the heart of the layman. That benefits only the common people, before their partisanship grows intense. As for the innovator, after he has learned even a little disputation, theology rarely benefits him: for if you silence him, he will not give up his position, and he ascribes the shortcoming to himself and supposes that someone else has some answer which he is unable to give, and you are merely confusing him by the strength of your argument.

As for the layman, when he has been turned away from the truth by some kind of disputation, it is possible to bring him back to it by something similar, before partisanship for his whims grows intense. Once their partisanship has grown intense, hope for them is lost, since partisanship is a cause that makes beliefs take root in the selves, and it is among the afflictions of the evil scholars: they go to extremes in partisanship for the truth and look at those who differ with them with the eye of contempt and belittlement, so that there arises from those who differ a claim to requital, confrontation, and treatment in kind, their motives multiply to seek support for falsehood, and their purpose in clinging to what they are ascribed to grows stronger. Had they come from the side of gentleness, mercy, and advice in private, not by way of partisanship and belittling, they would have succeeded in it. But since status does not stand except through having followers, and nothing wins over followers like partisanship, cursing, and abusing opponents, they took partisanship as their habit and tool and called it defending the religion and striving on behalf of the Muslims; yet in truth it is the destruction of people and the rooting of innovation
in the selves.

As for the disputed questions that have been introduced in these later times, in which have been innovated such writings, compilations, and disputations as have no like among the early generations, beware of hovering around them and avoid them as you would avoid deadly poison, for they are the incurable disease, and it is what has driven all the jurists back to seeking rivalry and boasting, as the details of its pitfalls and afflictions will come to you.
Perhaps this statement is heard from the one who says it, and then it is said: "People are enemies of what they are ignorant of." Do not think that; you have fallen upon one who knows.

So accept this advice from one who wasted his life in it for a time and surpassed the earlier generations in compilation, verification, disputation, and exposition, and then Allah inspired him with his right guidance and made him aware of its fault, so he abandoned it and occupied himself with himself. Let not the saying of one who says deceive you: "The legal opinion is the pillar of the Law, and its reasons are known only through the knowledge of disputation." For the reasons of the school are mentioned in the school, and anything beyond them is disputations that the earlier generations did not know, nor the Companions, though they were more knowledgeable than others about the reasons of legal opinions. Rather, besides being unhelpful in the knowledge of the school, it is harmful, spoiling the taste for jurisprudence. For that to which the intuition of the mufti attests, when his taste in jurisprudence is sound, cannot in most cases be made to proceed in accordance with the conditions of disputation. So whoever's nature has grown accustomed to the forms of disputation, his mind submits to the requirements of disputation and shrinks from submitting to the taste for jurisprudence. Only one who seeks fame and status occupies himself with it, and he pretends that he is seeking the reasons of the school, while his life may pass without his aspiration ever turning to the knowledge of the school. Be safe from the devils of the jinn and guard against the devils of mankind, for they have relieved the devils of the jinn of the toil of seducing and misleading. In sum, what is approved by the wise is that you imagine yourself alone in the world with Allah, with death, the presentation, the reckoning, Paradise, and the Fire before you, and reflect on what concerns you of what is before you, and leave aside everything else. And peace.

Some shaykh saw one of the scholars in a dream and said to him, "What has become of those branches of knowledge you used to dispute over and debate?" He stretched out his hand, blew into it, and said, "All of them have perished as scattered dust. I have benefited only from two rak'as that remained pure for me in the depth of the night."

In a hadith: "No people went astray after guidance they had been on except that they were given disputation" (١). Then he recited ⟦QS 43:58⟧. And in a hadith on the meaning of the saying of Allah Most High ⟦QS 3:7⟧ to the end of the ayah: they are the people of disputation whom Allah meant by His saying, Most High (٢). And one of the early generations said, "At the end of time there will be a people for whom the door of action is shut and the door of disputation is opened."

And in some reports: "You are in a time in which you have been inspired with action, and there will come a people who are inspired with disputation" (٣). And in the well-known report: "The most hated of people to Allah Most High is the most contentious adversary" (٤). And in the report: "No people took up speech except that they were denied action" (٥). And Allah knows best.

nilai.catatan: Judul bagian setia dan lengkap.
Tiga jenis ilmu, cakupan negasi, dan kalimat sambung "It is like" sesuai sumber.
Contoh sehat/indah, buruk, dan sedang (harta, keberanian) lengkap dan tepat.
Ilmu tercela, contoh sihir, jimat, perbintangan, dan alasan menyia-nyiakan umur sesuai sumber.
Mudaratnya melebihi yang diduga diperoleh; setia.
"the morbid matter increases" mengubah pelaku (orang itu yang menambah materi penyakit); "in the end" membaca "akhirah" sebagai "akhir"; selebihnya setia.
Kalimat syarat dan ketentuan meninggalkan dosa lahir-batin setia.
Urutan ilmu, larangan menghabiskan umur pada satu cabang, batas bahasa dan nahwu lengkap dan tepat.
"as compiled in al-Wasit" mengubah kalimat aktif (pelaku al-Wahidi tersirat) menjadi pasif tanpa pelaku; bilangan tepat.
Batas minimum hadits (dua Sahih, tashih salinan pada ahlinya) sesuai sumber.
Nama perawi sudah ditanggung pendahulu, tidak wajib hafal matan, batas sedang sesuai sumber.
Istiqsa hadits lengkap: kuat-lemah, jalur, keadaan perawi.
Bilangan dan judul kitab tepat, tetapi doa rahmat untuk al-Muzani tidak dalam kurung seperti glosarium.
"about" pada "about a hundred leaves" tidak ada di sumber; "argument" untuk al-mujadala tidak seragam dengan "disputation".
Pelaku pada rantai klausa (pihak yang berbeda, ulama jahat) terlacak benar; lengkap.
Penggalan lanjutan "in the selves" setia.
Perintah menjauhi khilafiyat, penyakit yang sukar disembuhkan, dan para fakih setia.
Kutipan peribahasa dan idiom penutup dibaca dengan makna tepat.
Pemilik pendapat, pembahasan fatwa dan khilaf, nasihat penutup setia.
Pelaku dialog mimpi (syekh bertanya, ulama menjawab) tidak tertukar; lengkap.
Placeholder, penanda kaki, dan lafaz ayat tidak diterjemahkan sesuai aturan.
"of people" menyempitkan "al-khalq" (makhluk); penanda dan penutup lengkap.
